rag_documents.title: Dealing with several Operators could use some advice
rag_documents.content:
Topic: Dealing with several Operators could use some advice

Author: Lundquist17
Date: 2025-03-30T15:38:39Z
Content: My mother passed away in Jan 2014, her mineral rights were split between me and another family member, recorded in march of 2015. Right off the bat, I noticed that the size of the checks for S&M Energy were different. My mother was averaging a certain amount when she was alive, while afterwards me and the other family member combined average about 2/3rds less then what my mother did though production was the same.
Then later while going through the numbers, I found a strange circumstance between a 2 month period of 2 check amount averages, right after her death.

Author: James_Garner1
Date: 2025-03-31T13:58:48Z
Content: You will need to start by methodically collecting all relevant data. List the county and State here for greater assistance. If you are in TX, then go to the TX RRC and start building your dataset. Create a plat covering your mineral ownership by using a screenshot from the RRC GIS information. Start to overlay the unit and permit information. Make sure to use API numbers and not well names since that can lead to confusion. API numbers can be tied directly directly tied to the company property numbers.

Author: Kbeth
Date: 2025-04-02T23:35:56Z
Content: I know from personal experience that trying to do all this is a daunting task.  For what’s it is worth, what I did when trying to get a handle on my mother’s mineral rights was to hire some knowledgeable help.  I realize pretty quickly that it was all over my head.  I have a couple of suggestions that might help:

Author: Lundquist17
Date: 2025-04-03T11:48:11Z
Content: I wish that I could hire somebody, and working 50 plus hours a week, bearly scrapping by, doesn’t leave alot of room or time for self education or research, but ive learned alot already. I seen something you wrote though, that tells you exactly understand. Alot of people I’ve talked to, really don’t. That Tracy is “Truly on our siide.”
There really is ive come to find, two sides. And it sucks. I just wanted to be able to trust people, these companies, to do the right thing. To be honest and open, to be fair, you know? Especially with some thing like family mineral rights that have passed on from geneation to generation. And I did truly trust them, for years. And maybe I’m being naive, or Pollyannaish or whatever, about how the world works, and maybe that’s a fault in me to a degree, I don’t know.
It just sucks. That those who are the most trusting, and often have the least of things in this world are so often taken advantage of by those who have the most. I just wish it wasn’t us versus them. I never wanted that, and I don’t think I’m unreasonable in disiring so.

Author: Kbeth
Date: 2025-04-03T18:17:26Z
Content: I couldn’t agree more.  It does suck.  My dad was in the oil patch as a geologist for decades and got screwed over so many times you can’t count.  The old saying in the oil biz is something like shake hands on a deal but be sure to count your fingers when it’s over.

Author: James_Garner1
Date: 2025-04-03T19:10:49Z
Content: @Lundquist17This is not a business for the “faint of heart”. Companies looking to lease or purchase your minerals have a duty to acquire/lease the interest at the least cost. With that said, they are not supposed to make representations that diminish the value of your property during negotiations; however, there are subjective ways to get around those limitations and some just ignore those limits.

Author: Lundquist17
Date: 2025-04-07T14:19:24Z
Content: Unfortunately, I’m not really talking about the evaluation of property or mineral rights with the goal to sell. I’m talking above monthly revenue from companies that are, and have already been paying on a check by check basis for the exreaction of the gas and oil.

Author: James_Garner1
Date: 2025-04-07T14:59:00Z
Content: The same advice applies to selling, leasing or revenue transactions.

Author: Lundquist17
Date: 2025-04-10T02:35:50Z
Content: Thats true, sorry if it seemed liked I was dismissing what you were saying. Just frustrated is all

rag_documents.title: Production Payment
rag_documents.content:
Topic: Production Payment

Author: Teddeshred
Date: 2025-05-21T19:04:46Z
Content: Does anyone have a copy of a lease, or an example of a lease, that is specifically a production payment? Meaning the lease was tied to a specific dollar amount and once satisfied, expires? Redact everything you’d like, all I am looking for is the language used to define terms. Thanks!

Author: Richard_Winblad
Date: 2025-05-22T18:44:24Z
Content: I have never heard of a oil and gas lease that allows recovery of the specific dollar amount.  Every lease I see has a clause that provides for the least to continue as long as there is production.

Author: Bob77
Date: 2025-05-22T19:42:28Z
Content: Ive seen this in mineral deeds, in the 40+ years Ive been around the industry, Ive never seen this for an OGL.  Not sure what you are trying to prove/disprove, but good luck!

Author: Teddeshred
Date: 2025-05-22T20:34:31Z
Content: From what I have been told, they were popular in deals around 1950s.

Author: TennisDaze
Date: 2025-05-28T02:37:23Z
Content: This is not an oil and gas lease.  It is an assignment of an existing oil and gas lease from the Assignor Lessee to 2 new lessees, Richardson and Bass, who were operators.  You can tell this because the original lessor is United States.  In addition to receiving some cash, the Assignor was to be be paid 3% of gross sales up to a total of $500 acre for net acres included in underlying lease.  Basically this is delayed purchase price because no well had been drilled.  If no well was ever drilled, the Seller Assignor would get nothing.

Author: Teddeshred
Date: 2025-05-28T21:30:57Z
Content: Thank you for that! I am new to all of this, trying to figure it out. In this assignment, the reference to the 1951 lease, I assume is between the US (original lessor) and the Assignor here in this document?

Author: Bob77
Date: 2025-05-28T21:32:12Z
Content: Like TD said above, this isnt a lease, its an assignment.  Basically they assigned the leasehold interest, withholding 3% interest of the payments until they recovered $500 per acre, which in 1952 was a good amount of money, Id assume.  Upon completion of payout of $500 per acre, all rights convey unto the Assignee and the assignment is null and void

rag_documents.title: Ancillary probate by oil companies
rag_documents.content:
Topic: Ancillary probate by oil companies

Author: Kathy_Mounts
Date: 2025-05-17T14:34:07Z
Content: My mother passed away this year.  She had mineral rights in New Mexico which she was a resident of at the time of her death. She had a will as well as TODD on her rights to be transferred to myself and my brother.  Which has been filed in Lea County. ,New Mexico.   One of the oil companies has the lease is requesting an ancillary probate.  Is this necessary??

Author: TennisDaze
Date: 2025-05-17T14:57:54Z
Content: Ancillary probate is usually done for nonresidents who owned NM property as they file probate in another state.  You need to consult a NM estate attorney to determine whether the filings are adequate under NM law.

Author: Jerry_Ithaca
Date: 2025-05-18T10:38:07Z
Content: In New Mexico a TODD it is effective immediately upon death. Much like a beneficiary  on a bank account. So it boils down to what an oil company will accept.

Author: mineralsjb2009
Date: 2025-05-18T14:09:36Z
Content: I’m not attorney (graduated from law school) and this isn’t legal advice. Please consult with a NM attorney. If you need references, I have several I can send.

Author: TennisDaze
Date: 2025-05-18T16:05:14Z
Content: Often these points are not understood by the particular individual (such as owner relations or D.O. analyst) at the oil company handling the title transfer.  He may not be aware of changes to state law or the difference between probate and ancillary probate.  So the title question may need to get up to the head of division orders or the legal department.  You can ask for the reason why the recorded TODD is not acceptable.  If they require probate which you do not otherwise need to file in NM, then your attorney will need to review and discuss with company.

Author: Jerry_Ithaca
Date: 2025-05-18T18:58:11Z
Content: The above description was the situation that I was in (Property in New Mexico, deceased owner lived in TX). The TODD was worded nearly identical to the deceased’s will. The oil company immediately accepted the TODD, ancillary probate was not requested by the oil company.

Author: SusanG46
Date: 2025-05-18T18:58:20Z
Content: My son and his became heirs to his grandmother’s estate, due to his father dying (intestate, he was not involved in their lives) prior his mother’s passing. His family lived in Texas. He was contacted by Spur Energy informing him of the property he inherited in Eddy County, but has yet to find a Will probated or a trust for his grandmother. Spur Energy is also saying he needs to do an ancillary probate. So can you share under the circumstances what his next step should be and share the names of some NM lawyers you would recommend?

Author: Kathy_Mounts
Date: 2025-05-18T18:58:29Z
Content: Thank.you. We have an attorney.  I will
contact the oil.company again.  I am amazed,how difficult they can be.  And I thought dealing with life insurance was difficult.

Author: Richard_Winblad
Date: 2025-05-19T18:25:35Z
Content: In some states there may be the need for an affidavit with a death certificate filed with a form referencing the TODD & legal description.  I don’t know about NM, but in Oklahoma there is a 9 month time limit to file the acceptance paperwork.  Visit with a NM atty.This post is not legal, tax or investment advice. Reading or responding to this post does not create an attorney/client relationship.

Author: sclausen
Date: 2025-05-26T19:12:27Z
Content: In cutting to the chase, you need to consult with an experienced NM probate attorney to determine what actually needs to be done.

Author: bparrish
Date: 2025-05-28T10:21:47Z
Content: I think in general oil companies are getting pickier about this.  My mom passed in 1995, and we’ve had several leases pay us on just seeing a copy of her will… her estate was not large enough to require probate in CA.  (mineral rights are in ND).  One of the companies (that leased to us in the past with no probate)… now will not pay us until we complete either an affidavit (two copies by non-relatives - and there is nobody left alive with the knowledge required, who could complete these)… or via probate… so we are working with a ND attorney to figure out what we have to do to complete probate in ND.

Author: TennisDaze
Date: 2025-05-28T13:15:59Z
Content: You are comparing two different standards.  The landman who leases on behalf of the oil company will sometimes base this on tracing heirs to get 100% of minerals under lease.  However, when the chain of title is reviewed by the attorneys who issue a drilling title opinion, they will note the gaps in deed records (failure to establish clear legal) for some heirs and require that the title be cleared before royalties are paid.  This is to ensure that the oil company does not suffer losses by paying royalties to Heir A and then have  Heir B appear and demand payment.   A non-probated will might have left the minerals to Son A and not to Daughter B.  After some point in time, it will be too late to file the will and the minerals will pass under real property intestacy statutes to both A and B.

Author: 4theRightChild
Date: 2025-05-27T17:18:41Z
Content: I’ve recently requested that a passage of an O&G lease be stricken out because it states ‘all other products’ extraction as part of the potential royalties. My idea was to obtain seperate leases on anything else they find.
Since I also requested as much post-production costs be withdrawn as possible the lease was changed to omit gas entirely as its “nominal yield” isnt even worth it compared to oil.
So apparently my lease is for oil only.

Author: M_Barnes
Date: 2025-05-27T18:32:49Z
Content: In my opinion, terrible idea to strike gas.  Gas often comes up with the oil as its bubbles help bring up the oil, so you need it in the lease.  Or condensate liquids come up with gas as part of the flow stream.   Think about Italian salad dressing.  All mixed together and only separate out if you let it settle.  And you definitely want to get paid on the gas.  Not all wells are just oil.  You would have a hard time getting separate leases for each product.  With a good attorney’s help, you can refine the 'All other products" clause on the lease.

Author: Bob77
Date: 2025-05-27T20:11:41Z
Content: To be blunt, youve read to many crazy conpsiracies on here/ or heard from friends neighbors to do something like that.  Im guessing you did this due to the uptick in lithium? Which is a completely different animal

rag_documents.content:
Topic: Leon County oil & gas lease 101 for beginner

Author: JRMJR
Date: 2025-03-09T22:59:28Z
Content: I have received a Mineral Lease offer from Comstock.
This new to me.
All that has been communicated from Comstock is: is a lease proposal stating, your prop is within the survey, your offer is “x” amount royalty, at “x” amount per NMA for a 3+2 lease, please sign and return.
This is a pool of property owners, and doesnt seem to be a large amount of money, so I am not considering attorney involvement.
Where do I start ?

Author: M_Barnes
Date: 2025-03-10T13:54:54Z
Content: Personally, do not agree to the extra two year option.  Ask for a higher royalty and ask for a higher bonus.  First offers tend to be lowball.  Not getting an attorney can cost you royalties in the long run.  If you only have a tiny bit of acreage, then you may not want one, but significant acreage would be important.  Do you understand every word in the contract you are about to sign?  If you only have an offer letter, I do not sign them.  I want the actual draft lease in my hands and want to understand every clause and its ramifications for the next 50 years.  Also, do not hand over a signed lease without getting paid that day.

Author: JRMJR
Date: 2025-03-11T20:24:31Z
Content: Thank you for the reply.
Where can I find a map of the well ?
Landman says no name or # has been given, I only have (2) survey I.D.'s

Author: M_Barnes
Date: 2025-03-13T14:00:04Z
Content: If they are at the leasing state, there is probably not a well name yet (or one that is public).  If you have the block, abstract and section, we can show you where you are located on a map.

Author: kborak
Date: 2025-03-14T10:14:04Z
Content: Very interesting. My family has interest with 6 wells in A-163 but we haven’t received anything. The wells we currently have there are smaller vertical wells that are at the end of their life. We are currently with another drilling company with them. Would be interesting to find out more of where Comstock is planning to run a future rig. We have interest with Comstock in Leon county in another abstract as well.

Author: M_Barnes
Date: 2025-03-14T13:12:43Z
Content: https://gis.rrc.texas.gov/GISViewer/A-163image1763×853 217 KB

Author: Itsbob
Date: 2025-04-15T19:36:14Z
Content: Oops! Just read this posting of yours which said, “do not hand over a signed lease without getting paid that day”.  I and my brothers just signed over a lease in substantial mineral rights, to explore on the promise of an offer letter which seemed legit and substantial as there has been very little interest in our sections in Crockett Co. Now we’re sweating out whether or not we’ll get the bonus payments offered and the time limit for their response is running out. What to do if…?

Author: M_Barnes
Date: 2025-04-15T19:59:52Z
Content: Welcome to the forum.  Some brokers work for the operators and you will get paid close to when they say they will pay.  Others are flippers and may file your lease before they pay you so that they can then flip the lease (usually to their benefit, not yours).  If they don’t find a buyer quickly, that is when they may not pay on time and getting a filed lease back out of the courthouse due to lack of payment can be difficult.  It is much safer to have your signed lease held by a third party such as a banker, attorney or accountant.  They will turn over the lease when the payment is made, so that the lease cannot be filed without payment.  It does take time to run the title, so that is what is supposed to be happening in the “in between time”.

Author: Itsbob
Date: 2025-04-15T22:50:56Z
Content: That is so reassuring what you wrote. It all seemed on the up and up, he had us forward the signed lease to the principle and a copy to him. I looked up the principle who is a very large private equity firm established in 2017 hdq in Dallas, then got a glimpse of their holdings all around our property so that made me/us feel more secure. Still, I feel like we sailed into unchartered waters. It appears he’s a broker for their accumulations in and around the county where our land is. I’ll let you know how it turns out.

Author: Mineral_Owner5
Date: 2025-04-18T16:05:41Z
Content: It depends upon it’s location#1. A 3 year lease is long enough. 1/4 cost free royalty. There are mineral buyers and a lot of others want to get into that play.
If you don’t ask you won’t get it.

Date: 2025-05-27T17:08:38Z
Content: If you have a producing well on the lease, then you may be held by the secondary term.  If you just inherited, you have to contact the operator and tell them in order to get into pay status.

rag_documents.title: Avoid self employment taxes
rag_documents.content:
Topic: Avoid self employment taxes

Author: Glrice65
Date: 2025-04-02T20:25:06Z
Content: I am an unleased Cotenant in Texas. The revenue is being reported as non employment income on my 1099 which is subject to self employment tax. Any ideas on how to avoid or minimize the self employment tax on this type of income?

Author: TennisDaze
Date: 2025-04-02T23:00:48Z
Content: As an individual, you will have to report on Schedule C.   Be sure to deduct all the JIB payments for well costs, and other direct costs such as postage.  You may be able to deduct a portion of your health insurance and your accounting fees.  Consult your CPA about this.

Author: Richard_Winblad
Date: 2025-04-02T23:35:32Z
Content: Visit with your CPA, I imagine that you need to report as royalty income.

Author: TennisDaze
Date: 2025-04-03T01:57:05Z
Content: Revenues from unleased minerals are treated for tax purposes as being a working interest.  After payout, the MI receives all the income and has to pay JIB costs.   The individual owner will report on Schedule C as self-employment income.  The mineral owner will receive a 1099-NEC from the oil company.

Author: Glrice65
Date: 2025-04-03T11:49:45Z
Content: Does dropping mineral rights into a trust avoid self employment income on unleased co tenant self employment income ?

Author: TennisDaze
Date: 2025-04-03T16:41:44Z
Content: I have no idea.  That is a question for your estate planning attorney and CPA, and any decision on a trust has long-term management, legal, tax and cost considerations.

Author: sclausen
Date: 2025-05-26T20:50:23Z
Content: There are many different types of trusts, which can have different tax consequences.  Ask your CPA and estate planning attorney for advice.  A revocable trust will not change the income tax result and neither will an IDGIT.

rag_documents.title: Capital Gains Taxes
rag_documents.content:
Topic: Capital Gains Taxes

Author: Polstead
Date: 2025-04-04T01:20:15Z
Content: I am selling my mineral rights. I was expecting to pay capital gains taxes on the full amount. But, a land expert said don’t do that. Those minerals have been there for centuries. I should determine the cost basis of the minerals for the day in 1996 when we purchased the property. He said there are no laws in Louisiana for assessing minerals, so I should make an estimate. He suggested something like saying the cost basis of the 80k sale at 56k, resulting in a capital gain of 24k. That would result in a federal tax of $3600 (15% of $24000) rather than 15% of 80k which would be $12000, a rather large savings. He thought that would be conservative enough to satisfy the IRS. He said he has seen several cases like this and never heard of the IRS challenging any of them. Does anybody out there have an opinion about this?

Author: TennisDaze
Date: 2025-04-04T01:57:37Z
Content: Your legal tax basis is the price you paid (or estate value if inherited) less all depletion deductions since 1996.  Your basis can be reduced to zero, but not below zero, by the depletion.  Your tax basis has nothing to do with a value for property tax purposes.

Author: Nick-TBM
Date: 2025-04-04T16:39:59Z
Content: I would caution you against this blanket advice. Go to a tax expert for tax advice.

Author: John_Murray
Date: 2025-04-04T17:56:19Z
Content: I think a lot of us are potentially facing this issue in the future. The problem is that a lot of these interests were purchased for almost nothing at the dawn of time and only became valuable when new drilling methods kicked in 15 or 20 years ago. It becomes even more complicated when the rights were dumped in a trust years ago and the stepped-up upon death basis calculations are clouded by multiple deaths in a survivor takes all trust situation.

Author: Nick-TBM
Date: 2025-04-04T18:03:59Z
Content: This is a valid assessment lol. Free advice isn’t always good advice. Someone above correctly mentioned the depreciation of an asset as well and if you are claiming a cost basis, this property may have been bought for 10,000 50 years ago, has depreciated over those years, and now you receive 100,000 for it… Why not take that as a personal tax at the lower 2.5% versus falsifying a capital gains. Sure the tax man may not get you, but they did get my man Capone.

Author: TennisDaze
Date: 2025-04-04T18:38:50Z
Content: The basis rules have been around for many decades.  It is just that most people ignore the rules or throw away all the paperwork, instead of carefully tracking basis.  Tracking means keeping record of original basis less any depletion - down to, but not below, zero. If you have a very low basis in minerals and give it to Child A, then A gets your basis (plus any gift tax paid to IRS but that is a different matter).  If Child A gets the minerals at your death, then A has basis of fair market value at your death.  If the minerals are placed in an irrevocable trust as part of a gift, then your basis carries over to the trust.  When the minerals are distributed to the beneficiaries, then they get the trust basis.  If minerals go into a testamentary trust (death), then the trust has basis at date of donor’s death.  That basis carries over to the ultimate beneficiaries.  There can be a couple differences for particular trust situations.  For example, if you put minerals into a living trust, then the trust is not really final until your death and its gets a stepped up basis at that time.  This should have been discussed in detail with both your estate attorney and CPA and then basis records maintained, by either the trustee for the trust to hand over to the beneficiaries or by the individual owner.  Bottom line is that if an individual or trust has owned the minerals for many decades and there has been a lot of production and depletion, then likely your basis is zero.  There are some different rules and calculations where the minerals are instead in a partnership or corporation.  It takes time and work to properly maintain detailed records.  If you do not want to do it yourself, then you should be paying your CPA or accountant to do that.

Date: 2025-07-03T01:20:37Z

rag_documents.content:
Topic: W. T. Rolph missing instruments from 1890's in Borden County, Tx

Author: Where.is.Rolph
Date: 2025-05-23T21:14:12Z
Content: I have been researching several parcels of land in Borden County, Tx for potential rights, and have come to a major gap in the early title during the 1890s. I worked on these exact tracts 14 years ago, and know and sort of remember what occurs, but do not remember the names, instruments bk & pg, and the amounts or rights retained. W. T. Rolph received 20 sections of land in Borden County during the 1890s through 4 separate instruments. The instruments are DR 2-256, 2-258, 2-261, 2-263. He then immediately leased all the acquired lands to Magnolia Cattle and Land Company in DR 2-266. The problem is, the numerous errors & missing entries in the Grantor/Grantee indices in Borden County in early title. I remember this from 14 years ago, and that there was a conveyance from Rolph to an entity/person. It is not logged in the direct Granter/Grantee book, but I remember once it was located years ago, it was logged in the reverse Grantee/Grantor book. I have already been through the reverse book looking at all of the grantors to the time of type writers, and have been unable to find the instrument because of the handwriting. All “known” siblings and heirs of W. T. Rolph have been searched to no avail. Through all these years of Texas, I know other people have either worked or come across these tracts and the W. T. Rolph dilemma. If anyone knows the instrument(s) from W. T. Rolph conveying to someone in Borden County, (not QCD instrument in 4-344 because this is not the correct lands), I’d like the information of the instrument. There is a separate chain from the grantor(s) that end up with R. H. Looney, but I remember when we worked this 14 years ago, the W. T. Rolph portion also eventually ends back with R. H. Looney. Finding the missing instrument from Rolph to ??? is what I need. Hopefully one of you has the instrument info handy.

Author: TennisDaze
Date: 2025-05-23T21:33:09Z
Content: You can find them on Texasfile which has deeds back to 1877.  You can register and add funds by credit card.  Fee is $1 per page to purchase.   Once you register, for example, enter 2 in Volume box and 256 in Page box and search.  It will come up as Not Indexed for Grantor and for Grantee names.  That is why you cannot search by name.  Purchase and download the original handwritten deed.

Author: Where.is.Rolph
Date: 2025-05-26T19:29:15Z
Content: Thank you for the information & instructions pertaining to the instruments on Texasfile. I have now gotten a copy of all of these instruments that quit claim into W. T. Rolph in: DR 2-256, 2-258, 2-261, 2-263. As well as the subsequent Lease from W. T. Rolph to the Magnolian Land & Cattle Company for all of the lands. I have gone through each of the hand written instruments to find a name, entity name that I might be able to research to link the ownership.
My question is in regards to the the instrument where the ownership of the described lands go from W. T. Rolph’s name to another entity or person. This is the instrument of record in Borden County that needs to found. Finding the missing instrument from Rolph to ??? is what I need. Hopefully one of you has the instrument info handy.

rag_documents.title: Having a good lease - Alabama Ferry field
rag_documents.content:
Topic: Having a good lease - Alabama Ferry field

Author: Akranch
Date: 2025-04-15T01:46:41Z
Content: I know a few of you have seen me post pictures and videos from this Alabama ferry field in SE leon county. I had to go on my neighbors property today to check on something and seen this while i was there. The neighbor never noticed this and he doesn’t have any minerals so he never looks at this well. Hopefully this will be our white bronco on getting our minerals back. This field has been sitting for years with no production and everytime the RRC starts anything the owner pops out of a hole and pays them off. This is the third time within a year something like this happened. Most people in this area (my parents as well) signed a pretty weak lease in the early 80’s. I will be contacting the RRC about this.20250414_1958551920×1440 431 KB

Author: Jimmy
Date: 2025-04-16T00:14:35Z
Content: That’s not good, try some dawn soap and lots of hay and white sand, on it , omy, stay safe! OSHA and the epa ? Thanks for sharing! Interesting

Author: Akranch
Date: 2025-04-16T04:18:23Z
Content: RRC came out today and inspected it. They are schedule to plug this one since the owner is no where to be found. We are hoping others will in plugged as well and our minerals released because of no production for over the last 12 months. Most of these wells hasn’t produced anything in several years. I also took the field guy to a well he didn’t even know it was there. Half these wells in this field isn’t even mapped on the RRC mapping. Then getting to them you have to walk to because either the creeks washed out the crossing or the roads to them are grown up. I am meeting with the district manager out of Henderson Thursday to show him other problem wells in this field. People on the northern side of this field are have oil show up in their drinking water. Luckily we haven’t had this issue here yet. But if these wells are taken care of we could.

Author: Mineral_Owner5
Date: 2025-04-21T14:53:23Z
Content: You and your neighbors may need to contact the Austin Office of the Texas Railroad Commission along with Certified Letters. return receipt requested since the Henderson Office won’t do anything. I believe the State or the Federal Govt. can come up with the money. All this operator is doing is trying to hold (HBP) these leases to sell for another oil and gas play. Maybe the Comstock Play or the other players.

Author: Akranch
Date: 2025-04-22T14:36:02Z
Content: I am working on that now. I also contacted Mr. Dunlap that ran for commissioner this past election. He got me in contact with a houston news paper.  We are about to expose just how screw up the RRC is on these well clean ups are. Most of the field guys try to do their jobs but Austin sits on their butts and do nothing. They just bandaid these cleans for a bigger problem in the future all over the state. If they are really about clean and water they wouldn’t have so many orphan weĺls around the state. They let companies leave these problems when they should hold the accountable.

Author: Mineral_Owner5
Date: 2025-04-28T01:56:09Z
Content: What about the operation that has these rights HBP’ed that has their gathering system on Hwy 7 west of Centerville? Go to the App. District and see who is paying property tax on it and their address. If I owned mineral rights in this water flood mess I would hire a law firm to get my mineral rights released before they sell or lease them for the deep gas play by Comstock and others.

Author: Akranch
Date: 2025-04-29T14:24:07Z
Content: That was Lasmo Energy on 7. They have some wells producing but not many. With everyone tied up in these units from the water floods in our area i have to get everyone to go along. The crazy thing is no one wants to rock the boat to get the minerals back. I do have over 300 mineral acres no tied up in this field so if someone comes leasing i will update it and maybe work a deal with the company leasing to include my other land.

Author: Kitchen
Date: 2025-04-29T18:33:00Z
Content: I view any leak as lost revenue. Force the RRC to force the operator to clean it up. The RRC has funds for emergencies also.

Author: Akranch
Date: 2025-04-30T04:06:44Z
Content: Thats what got me. You would think the RRC would have sold the oil in these tanks to be use to clean this up. I asked the field clean up guy about damages payment and he said the state doesn’t pay damage payments. They took all the oil soak soil and dumped it inside the firewall. Which then took up space for the oil to stay inside the firewall with it still leaking out. I asked the guy what happens if we get a hurricane here and it dumps several inches of rain and causes the oil and water to overflow the firewall. He said lets just hope that doesn’t happen. They are sure playing with fire. It this place gets hit by another lightning strike it wiĺl be a major fire.

Author: Mineral_Owner5
Date: 2025-04-30T13:30:16Z
Content: The RRC and TxDOT are still DEI type hires. If you report them not taking care of a problem it’s like the “FOX Guarding the HEN HOUSE”. They are policing themselves! You might try making a trip to the Austin Office and get a name of a person that may ultimately get something done.

Author: Akranch
Date: 2025-05-02T04:15:04Z
Content: I have talked to a couple of landowners about making a trip to Austin. One landowner doesn’t have any mineral rights and raises game deer. He’s had issues with game dèer getting into the oil that leaked off the location into his pasture last year. I am hoping i can get more people involved and make a bigger statement on getting things clean up.

Author: Akranch
Date: 2025-05-02T04:21:00Z
Content: 20250424_1000191920×1440 572 KB20250419_1027111920×2560 1.18 MB20250424_1001271920×1440 489 KB

Author: TennisDaze
Date: 2025-05-02T16:59:09Z
Content: The weak lease is not the problem.  It is that RRC has policy of not ordering pluggings for inactive wells, regardless of time.  How many wells are involved?  Are any of these wells on the Oil Field Cleanup - State Well Pluggings Remaining by District and what is the Priority listing?  There is a specific complaint process to handle these wells which will get attention.https://www.rrc.texas.gov/media/scngdype/wells-remaining-12-16-2024-pdf.pdfOr are the wells only listed as orphan wells?https://webapps2.rrc.texas.gov/EWA/orphanWellQueryAction.doIf they are not on either list, then check the RRC wellbore status to see if they have listed operator.

Author: Mineral_Owner5
Date: 2025-05-03T16:02:47Z
Content: Great Post, thanks! I suspect that the operator is only holding this old dead water flood project so that they can lease it for the Haynesville/Bossier Play that is moving south and east in Leon, Anderson and Houston County as well as Leon County.

Author: Akranch
Date: 2025-05-03T23:41:17Z
Content: Its around 1,400 wells that in the water flood program. Most of these wells still have tanks, line heater and heater trèe but the pump jacks were moved out. Some of them has a sand plug in them, and the rest are open. I got words yesterday the RRC will be cleaning up the injection station thats had these oil leak in September. Now if they really do it i want hold my breath. I finally got some ranchers in the area pushing as well on getting things cleaned up on their locations. Its only taken 10 years of calling, emails, and taking pictures of these issues that come up for them to finally say they will do it.

Author: TennisDaze
Date: 2025-05-04T18:20:03Z
Content: Maybe or maybe not.  In many old fields, the leases have been depth-severed and the deep-rights holders are not the same as the shallow-rights holders. The incentive here to keep ‘operating’ may be to avoid or delay the RRC-estimated $100,000 per well plugging cost.  By failing to require operators to plug wells which have not produced for decades, ultimately operations are assigned to small companies with few assets or the operators just go out of business.  Then RRC has to pay plugging costs.  But RRC does not clean up the all the surface, leaving surface owners with damaged land.

Author: Phil_Sartin
Date: 2025-05-04T18:33:23Z
Content: How could a performance bond protect the landowner and the taxpayers for being responsible for ecological disasters such as in the Alabama Ferry field?  Obviously, it’s too late for this field.

Author: TennisDaze
Date: 2025-05-04T23:26:04Z
Content: The bonds or cash deposits required by RRC for operators will not cover plugging costs for multiple wells.  Real problem is that RRC does not require nonproducing wells to be plugged as long as the lease has not expired, even after decades.  So 1,000s of old wells are sitting out there.  Then operator goes out of business, whether by death of owner or bankruptcy or etc and taxpayers and surface owners are left holding the bag.  Around 2010 the RRC started requiring plugging schedules for wells that were not producing for 5+ years.  That was overruled whether by inside RRC or by Commissioners and so here you have this disaster.  Meanwhile plugging costs are way up and so the RRC can never get ahead of needs.

Author: Akranch
Date: 2025-05-06T10:51:19Z
Content: This is crazy. Hilcorp was the last major operator of this field. They sold it to a company called Newco then this company officials spilt and they fourmed Geohydro. Then it split again and one guy took it over and called his company Texas Tea black gold. He’s  from Mexico and now he’s no where to be found. Its crazy they can’t come back on hilcorp for leaving this field like this. It not like they are out of business since Comstock just bought hilcorp interest in minerals in the western part of the county. Then they are the largest hold in the Alaska field now. All hilcorp did here was milk what they could from this field in the 10+ years they had it and leave this all behind. They owned it in 2015 when this injection station was hit by lightning. Then they never reported to the RRC. I called our field guy and he was totally caught off guard about it.

Author: Bembo
Date: 2025-05-15T05:15:43Z
Content: You may want to look up Rep. Darby’s HB 5568 regarding orphaned oil and gas wells.

rag_documents.title: Inherited Mineral rights are in Stock form?
rag_documents.content:
Topic: Inherited Mineral rights are in Stock form?

Author: brenda.birdie
Date: 2025-04-25T12:27:49Z
Content: I was of the understanding that I inherited Mineral rights in the Utica Shale, Southeastern part of Ohio. I was sent 170 shares of stock from Mid-Ohio Coal company. So my question is do I own Mineral rights and how do I find out more information or Do I just own stock in a company that owns the Mineral rights? I know this is vague but I’m not sure what I’m allowed to say on the forum. The Well is being drilled and producing but I only get a small dividend check and I want to find out if this is normal?

Author: M_Barnes
Date: 2025-04-25T12:52:27Z
Content: Sounds like you only have stock in the company.  For mineral rights, you would have to inherit a deed through a probate.

Author: sclausen
Date: 2025-05-26T19:27:34Z
Content: Based on your information, the stock is intangible personal property; you inherited no mineral property.

rag_documents.title: Minimum Oil Production to Continue Pumping
rag_documents.content:
Topic: Minimum Oil Production to Continue Pumping

Author: Jerry_Ithaca
Date: 2025-05-08T13:47:31Z
Content: I have a very general question. At what level of production of a horizontal fractured well is it no longer worthwhile or when would a producer stop pumping? I understand wells can be reworked, but at what point is a well dead?

Author: D_Wells
Date: 2025-05-10T21:53:49Z
Content: It’s a matter of economics.  It will depend on whether the well has paid out (broken even) or not.  Is there a net revenue after the sale of the product and the cost of operating the well?  Does maintaining the lease by operating the well have a future value?  These are questions, among others, the operator considers when deciding whether plug and abandon.

Author: Mineral_Owner5
Date: 2025-05-11T19:19:58Z
Content: It is important to have a minimum royalty clause in your leases. What is important is what is important to you and your families interest. It’s important to not be HBPed with practically no production. Otherwise you deeded them your mineral rights.

Author: M_Barnes
Date: 2025-05-12T13:48:29Z
Content: “Otherwise you deeded them your mineral rights” is an incorrect statement.  I think what you really meant is to put a limited time frame on a shut in or limit the lease to “economically paying quantities” of production.  The lease is not a deed.

Author: Jerry_Ithaca
Date: 2025-05-12T14:59:01Z
Content: Did some chatGBT stuff on the life of the wells of interest and it thru out a 100 barrels per month minimum to be financially worthwhile to continue pumping. Is that even in the ball park, chat GBT CAN be off in left field sometimes

Author: M_Barnes
Date: 2025-05-12T16:13:50Z
Content: Depending upon the operator, they may hang onto a well that is below the economic limit because they have a strategy in the area and want to keep the lease active.  We saw that a lot with uneconomic vertical wells at 1/8th being held until a horizontal was drilled because they wanted to keep HBP leases at 1/8th and not lease again when competitive leasing royalties might have been at 1/5th or 1/4th.

Author: Bob77
Date: 2025-05-13T02:33:34Z
Content: It all depends on the area.  If its an active area, a company will hold the acreage as long as they can by showing marginal production or paying the 1$ per ace per year and a mixture of both.  It has nothing to do with how much they are making off it now, its what they can get from selling the leases they have of doing a wellbore assignment while keeping a large override for a larger company to come in an drill 1-2 wells on top of them.  It makes 0 financial sense for the company to shut in the well if theres activity in the area.

Author: Mineral_Owner5
Date: 2025-05-26T16:40:21Z
Content: If a mineral owner signed a lease with a vertical Pugh clause that states to the “deepest depth drilled” and they drill a 20,000 well and then produce at 8,000 ft. They are HBP’ed down to the base of the “deepest depth drilled”!

posts.author: Jerry_Ithaca
posts.content: I have a very general question. At what level of production of a horizontal fractured well is it no longer worthwhile or when would a producer stop pumping? I understand wells can be reworked, but at what point is a well dead?

posts.author: D_Wells
posts.content: It’s a matter of economics.  It will depend on whether the well has paid out (broken even) or not.  Is there a net revenue after the sale of the product and the cost of operating the well?  Does maintaining the lease by operating the well have a future value?  These are questions, among others, the operator considers when deciding whether plug and abandon.

posts.author: Mineral_Owner5
posts.content: It is important to have a minimum royalty clause in your leases. What is important is what is important to you and your families interest. It’s important to not be HBPed with practically no production. Otherwise you deeded them your mineral rights.

posts.author: M_Barnes
posts.content: “Otherwise you deeded them your mineral rights” is an incorrect statement.  I think what you really meant is to put a limited time frame on a shut in or limit the lease to “economically paying quantities” of production.  The lease is not a deed.

posts.content: Did some chatGBT stuff on the life of the wells of interest and it thru out a 100 barrels per month minimum to be financially worthwhile to continue pumping. Is that even in the ball park, chat GBT CAN be off in left field sometimes

rag_documents.title: Inheritance, Apache buyout
rag_documents.content:
Topic: Inheritance, Apache buyout

Author: TConeFamily
Date: 2025-05-23T21:09:12Z
Content: A relative passed away 2 years ago. She left me mineral rights and I am familiar with their actual location, having grown up on or near the land they’re associated with. Since the Apache buyout, still no checks have been issued due to new costs and changes, taxes, etc. I received an offer to buy that I’m considering seriously. My question is two parts:

Author: Rock_Man
Date: 2025-05-23T21:36:14Z
Content: To properly evaluate any possible sale value for your mineral rights, one has to know a lot more information.

Author: Helen_Baldwin
Date: 2025-05-23T22:16:30Z
Content: An issue with the transfer of ownership from your relative’s estate to you, or a question about the percent ownership could be interfering with your payments.
Consider hiring an oil and gas attorney to learn about your gift before making any decision. My family and I have confidence in Wade Caldwell, oil and gas attorney, whose firm has helped us for many years.

Author: Roxane_Thomas
Date: 2025-05-23T22:46:41Z
Content: I second Wade Caldwell’s firm.  We recently sold some of our interests and they were able to shop us around.  We received 4 times the highest offer we were given without an attorney.

Author: Brenda_Johnson
Date: 2025-05-24T05:14:08Z
Content: I don’t know what the value of your mineral rights are at present time.  I was getting $150/month for my royalties every month for over 30 years.  They have gone up to over $2000/month.  Not every area is the same.  But, I have always been told to NOT sell.  I don’t think you’ll get payment for the 2 yr. period by selling it.  Whatever the offer is, it’s probably worth 25% of what it’s really worth.  Try to hang on to it if you can.  My opinion, I’m not an expert.  But I’ve negotiated many leases for my minerals.

Author: BlackGold
Date: 2025-05-25T23:48:00Z
Content: My thought is that you probably want to wait to sell until you start getting checks again.  Most buyers will want to know and will value your rights based on production or potential production.  So no revenue stream make it more difficult and perhaps at a lower price.  Instead of contacting or contracting with individual mineral buyers, there might be two places to start.  One is the producer themselves since they should have a very good idea of the value.  The other option would be one of the auction houses.  Why get offers from 2-3 random people when an auction house might get 100.  MCEE is one.  Oil and Gas Clearing House is another.  There are probably others.

Author: UncleJed
Date: 2025-05-20T23:45:01Z
Content: We received an offer from Antero and countered with 1.) 20% royalty on all oil, gas, and NGL’s. 2.) No Post Production Costs 3.) $4000/acre bonus 4.) Terms of the lease reduced from 5 years to 3. Here was his response:
I am presently working with 9 lessors that have lawyered up, and the ask is 20.0%. (As the Attorneys want their piece of the pie) They have been sitting as denied sense August 2024 as Antero is not giving 20.00%. On that alone, if I take your offer to Denver Office for approval,  they are just going to park it as denied.

Author: James_Garner1
Date: 2025-05-25T20:43:13Z
Content: Negotiations can be rough and tumble. Companies know their timelines, regulatory limits and competition, while most mineral owners do not place the proper weight on research and patience, Your minerals are perpetual, while their leasehold has a limited term. Net revenue can be negotiated through the methods you have suggested, but be open to accomplishing the same through an alternate method. Companies want the best net revenue for them and will dangle bonus money to influence you to a quicker and less informed decision. This does not directly answer your question, but I hope it provides assistance.

Author: swylie76
Date: 2025-05-20T13:42:58Z
Content: Good morning, our family was contacted back in 2020 by a rep from Callon Petroleum, about mineral rights owned my my husband and his brother that we are unaware of. They were working on figuring out any other heirs and a possible lease offer, however Biden was elected and everything stopped. Their family was big in Texas years ago. Wondering if anyone can suggest who we can contact to try to find this information out for ourselves? No really sure where to start.

Author: M_Barnes
Date: 2025-05-20T18:05:17Z
Content: Welcome to the forum.You can start with the Mineral Help tab above that gives an overview of the business.  Post a query in the county where your mineral rights are.  Give your township, range and section (or Block, abstract and section in TX).  I am assuming you are in Texas.  You can do some searching onwww.Texasfile.comfor your family names.  It is free to look and minimal to print.

Author: James_Garner1
Date: 2025-05-20T19:18:40Z
Content: How about starting the discussion at NARO about developing a YouTube series on the basics of mineral management and research? I would guess you could get TexasFile and OKCountyRecords to provide a user video for their systems also.

Author: M_Barnes
Date: 2025-05-20T19:38:10Z
Content: NARO (National Association of Royalty Owners) already has multiple webinars on the basics of mineral management on our YouTube private site.  We had a special series last year by all of the state chapter presidents on their own webinars telling how to find data on their respective states.  We have webinars on Division Orders, statement reviews, geology and more coming this year on more specialized topics.  A list is available on the member resources pages on the NARO website.www.naro-us.org.  We also have a new excellent minerals management handbook which we use in our Minerals Management classes.  They are taught at the various state conventions.

Author: James_Garner1
Date: 2025-05-20T20:01:17Z
Content: Great information, thank you. I hope this can be helpful to many of the new or wondering members on this forum.

Author: Bob77
Date: 2025-05-20T20:04:55Z
Content: Biden being elected had nothing to do with your current problem
What are you trying to learn? If you were contacted in 2020 and havent been contacted since, it just might be due to where your minerals are located, which mineral owners hate to hear and struggle with.As far as “learning”.  Pretty much all the counties that have oil and gas activity are now all online.  You can search whatever counties you are interested in and search your husbands name, parents or his last name to see what he owns and then take the legal descriptions found, if any, and search recent leasing or drilling.

Author: James_Garner1
Date: 2025-05-25T20:42:58Z
Content: Callon was doing quite a bit during that time period. They had capital issues, completed acquisitions, and were eventually acquired by Apache in 2024. There are times when company focus changes and your area is archived for another time. This is not a political statement, US oil production went to its highest point during Biden. His admin had very little to do with that accomplishment. Tangential issues can lead to poor associations.

rag_documents.title: How do we find if they plan to drill
rag_documents.content:
Topic: How do we find if they plan to drill

Author: Beck
Date: 2025-05-19T18:10:09Z
Content: We just signed lease on our mineral rights in Custer County and now a company is offering to buy our mineral rights.  How do we find if or when they plan to drill - or what value of mineral rights are?  the Landowner/Oil Company says the offer is low ball - so wondering if we should sell or hold?  Section 34-1 Township 13N Range 16W

Author: M_Barnes
Date: 2025-05-20T17:40:49Z
Content: You can watch for permits using the Oklahoma Corporation well records site.  Check not only your section, but the ones immediately to your north and south as locations are not always in the section they plan to perforate.

Author: Bob77
Date: 2025-05-20T20:31:56Z
Content: If you have a magic 8 ball, ask if they will drill, shake it and see what the response is.  Unfortuntely theres no way of finding out if they will drill a well, especially a newly taken OGL. Ive had some properties where Ive signed 4 OGL’s that still havent been drilled. Its the most frustrating part of being a mineral owner as you never know if they will drill the well or it they do and they file a 6 well incresed density and they drill 1 well, will they drill another well, 5 more or none.  I used to tell my now deceased wife, going to the PO Box each Thursday was like the kids on Christmas morning, never know what youre going to open uo, but when you get the paperwork they are drilling, its like Santa gave you everything you wanted!

Author: Terrel_Shields
Date: 2025-05-24T23:06:25Z
Content: Mineral deeds are subject to deed tax stamps in Oklahoma. The rate in OK is $1.50 per $1,000.  So if the deed stamps are $15, the sale price was $10,000. Go to the courthouse and pull recent deeds (they are probably on line in the courthouse clerks office)… Look for deeds that state the actual NET MINERAL ACRES. That will tell you what they paid per acre.

Author: Terrel_Shields
Date: 2025-05-25T20:02:08Z
Content: This shows you what a usable mineral deed looks like - not all deeds will give the net mineral acreage. Hopefully this will attach - if not I will link it to my website.custer county deed903×511 146 KB

Author: Shawn_Orton
Date: 2025-05-10T21:50:21Z
Content: Interesting! I too have been approached to purchase a leasehold by same company! My property is Sec 20 Block 42 Township 2 south. I basically was raised to never sell mineral rights! But this property would have me as a working interest partner. Curious if you decided to sell?

Author: AJ11
Date: 2025-05-12T16:52:10Z
Content: Does “working interest partner” mean you would be going into business with individuals you have never met? Would a conventional lessor to lessee oil and gas lease (approved by your o&g attorney) be an easier path to follow?  I asked AI for information about working interest partner in an oil well and this was part of the response:  “Unlike a royalty interest owner—who earns a portion of the profits without covering any costs—a working interest partner is financially responsible for things like drilling, equipment, and maintenance. Their share of the profits depends on their percentage of ownership in the well.”

Author: Shawn_Orton
Date: 2025-05-12T17:46:50Z
Content: Basically, I would not see any monies for a long time since I wouldn’t be able to pay up front costs. Id be a JIB(joint interest billing) owner! Until the production pays off my debt… any monies would be withheld. It could be years before I get a check! But I was raised to never sell mineral interests. Sadly Im not a royalty owner on this property.

Author: AJ11
Date: 2025-05-13T02:34:48Z
Content: Do you own minerals in the parcel description you shared? If not, what sort of ownership do you have? If you own minerals, why would you not simply lease your minerals to the company with a traditional oil and gas lease (approved by your attorney)?

rag_documents.content:
Topic: STARR county lost mineral rights

Author: TonnyT
Date: 2025-05-16T02:18:49Z
Content: Ok so my wife and her mother have done most of the leg work getting everything they need for their great great great grandfathers property. they even have a copy of the original “porciones” when land was gifted as wedding presents. We even have court papers from 2009 of some lawyer trying to take over the property but her grandfather was fighting it and won at the time. we can’t really make sense of the papers.
the thing is we called to Starr County court, tax, etc offices. one person told us that the parcels were “moved” which doesn’t sound right. they give us an address to a PO box almost 45 minutes away that belonged to her grandmother and the other address to a random house in town. a lawyer told us we need to find the address before they can do anything. from what my mother-in-law is telling me, her cousin is already collection royalties from his inherited land which has pipe running over or in it. He isnt much help since we have our own process to go through.

Author: Kitchen
Date: 2025-05-19T17:36:33Z
Content: You need to contact the Starr County Appraisal District and ask them to provide you the property / parcel information they have on file. Usually they can print or email to this to you as a “property card” which is a summary of all of the information about the property. That will have a legal description, which is what you are really looking for. Many properties do not have street / situs addresses assigned. Every property has a legal description.

Author: TonnyT
Date: 2025-05-19T19:55:09Z
Content: Thank you for the reply, we did go to the appraisal district WITH documented proof that my wifes family is the eirs. The appraisal district as giving alot of push back and said that the property was an address IN a neighborhood with a small house on it. which after some research shows as a house my mother-n-laws grandmother lived in at one time. Heres the thing, they say that the taxes is delinquient for that property. BUT it appears as the house is currently occupied BY SOMEONE.

Author: M_Barnes
Date: 2025-05-24T15:21:26Z
Content: Have you triedwww.Texasfile.comto see if there is any information there?  It is free to look.  Small fee to print.

rag_documents.content:
Topic: Stephens County OK offer

Author: User1982
Date: 2025-05-23T21:05:08Z
Content: Someone made an offer for my mineral rights in Stephens County that I inherited. How can I make sure it’s a good offer?

Author: LorraineD
Date: 2025-05-23T23:28:03Z
Content: You may want to sell, but in my experience those people want to grab your mineral rights at a low price because they are likely to be getting those royalties in perpetuity.
I let mine ride and when I get a little check, I kiss it, look up and say: “Thank you Mother”.
You can have them direct deposited into your bank or credit union account and it’s just, in my case, a little something that is better than a little nothing.
I get those solicitations to sell several times a year. I throw them away.
All the best to you.

Author: Michael_Hutchison1
Date: 2025-05-24T00:09:37Z
Content: Everyone’s situation is different. It depends on the future value of your current wells and the possibility of more wells in the future. Age and family dynamics can also be an important factor. Several years ago, already in my seventies, I got an offer that very well could’ve been more money than I would see in royalties in my lifetime. I had a good use for the money so I agreed to sell part of my acreage. I never looked back.

Author: M_Barnes
Date: 2025-05-24T13:46:16Z
Content: Welcome to the forum.All about location and where the next drilling will head.  Most offers come before drilling and they are likely to be lowball to see who will bite without negotiating.  If you share your location, we can help with surrounding activity and then you will have more information for your decision.  You can sell all, sell a portion or sit back and wait for the future to unfold.

Author: Tom_Ed_Moore
Date: 2025-05-24T14:19:06Z
Content: Continental sent me a propasal for the War Pig. 16 & 21 7N 5W Grady County, OK. Will wait for pooling. The well has been drilled

Author: M_Barnes
Date: 2025-05-24T15:14:42Z
Content: Tom,
If you already had horizontal wells in your sections, you are already held by production on those horizons if pooled and all horizons if you were leased with no depth clause.  Were you offered a lease on the War Pig?  It is planned to be in the Atoka. It was spud in mid-April.

Date: 2025-05-02T15:03:36Z
Content: Never sell your minerals more specifically if they are coming to you. They know its more money worth of natural gas than they will pay you. Plus you lose your rights on these wells they will drill.

Date: 2025-05-02T15:25:32Z
Content: You have now been introduced to “New Age” mineral buyers.The fire out shotgun offers, hope for a response, and then try to figure out the validity of their offer if you respond.

Author: Alan_Herrington
Date: 2025-05-02T18:00:51Z
Content: Comstock’s Freestone County well, the Olajuwon 1H, was discussed during their Q1 2025 earnings conference call yesterday.  The well went into production in April, and tested at 41,000 MCF, indicating it is a really good well. This well is located 24 miles away from their nearest prior well, so Comstock has now “proven” an area that stretches 45 miles from Robertson into Freestone.  The well is in the middle of a 30-mile wide area that Comstock has leased.

rag_documents.content:
Topic: Identifying the well i am waiting on

Author: rrhodes09
Date: 2025-05-21T19:05:42Z
Content: I inherited mineral rights and signed a lease with Surprise Valley last June. Most all the information I had  was from my father (also a partial mineral right owner) however he passed away last year. I am hoping someone might be able to help me identify the well  I am waiting on so I can follow the updates that pertain to our lease.

Author: TennisDaze
Date: 2025-05-21T23:05:19Z
Content: You need to post the legal description of the tract of land in the lease. Most likely the primary term (time to drill) is 3 years and so permits may not yet be filed.  Surprise Valley Resources is a company which leases on behalf of oil companies, so your lease will have been assigned to another company.  Most recently Surprise Valley has been assigning to Comstock Oil.& Gas Co.  This can be verified in the Leon County deed records.

Author: rrhodes09
Date: 2025-05-22T18:46:43Z
Content: Thomas Toby Sur A- 0885 71.049 is the legal description from the lease I signed. It also mentions Sulphur River Exploration.  I do believe it is related to Comstock from the info I had before my father passed.

Author: Bembo
Date: 2025-05-23T01:16:15Z
Content: If you will go to the railroad commission gis viewer and put in the api # 289-32192, it will locate the Williams RM lease. Click on the drilling permit link, go down the page until you see the Williams RM 1H well location plat. It will show you where this lease is in relation to A-885. Hope this is helpful.

rag_documents.title: Shut In Limitations?
rag_documents.content:
Topic: Shut In Limitations?

Author: lwd
Date: 2025-05-20T15:35:21Z
Content: Lease from 2010 was not favorable to lessor and no time limit listed for shut in.  Last production was in 2017 and have received a shut in payment annually since.  Can a shut in last until well is closed?  What if shut in payment isn’t cashed? Can this last indefinitely?

Author: M_Barnes
Date: 2025-05-20T17:30:35Z
Content: Welcome to the forum. Unfortunately, a shut in clause with no time limits can last indefinitely.  I inherited some that have been dragging on for decades.  It can be expensive to try (and frequently doomed to fail) to break a lease with that type of clause.  If you don’t cash the check, you are probably just missing out on some extra cash.

Author: lwd
Date: 2025-05-21T19:04:36Z
Content: Thank you for the information and sharing your personal experience

Author: Richard_Winblad
Date: 2025-05-22T18:47:19Z
Content: When signing a new lease, it is important to have a limitation on the number of years  shut in rights can last.

rag_documents.title: Legality of Quit Claim Deed for transferring mineral rights
rag_documents.content:
Topic: Legality of Quit Claim Deed for transferring mineral rights

Author: kiheiman
Date: 2025-02-24T18:52:14Z
Content: My Dad prepared a Quit Claim Deed in 2007 to transfer his New Mexico mineral rights to his living trust.  The deed was signed, notarized, and delivered to the grantee (my Mom).  My Dad died in early 2008.  My Mom recorded the Quit Claim deed in late 2008 in the appropriate NM county courthouse.  She was the surviving Trustee.  My Mom died in 2023. Is it safe to assume that the NM mineral rights are assets of the trust and that the first successor trustee can convey the mineral rights to the trust beneficiaries via Quit Claim deeds?

Author: Richard_Winblad
Date: 2025-02-24T21:24:30Z
Content: You will need a New Mexico licensed attorney to chime in on this.  States have different requirements regarding whether delivery is sufficient or whether recording prior to death is necessary.

Author: kiheiman
Date: 2025-02-25T13:33:20Z
Content: Here is my challenge.  I would like to find a lawyer in New Mexico (Eddy Country) and Oklahoma (Jackson Country), where I could sit down with them for a max of two hours and get answers to my questions - and pay a reasonable fee for their time.  I have no idea where to find such lawyers.  We tried to find a lawyer in Lubbock, Texas for  similar questions on Texas farm mineral rights.  They wanted $6K to $8K to take a quick look at the situation.  IMHO, that is not reasonable.

Author: Mineral_Owner5
Date: 2025-02-25T16:08:37Z
Content: Are the mineral rights leased or are they producing? If they are producing is there money held by the State of New Mexico?

Author: Permian
Date: 2025-02-25T17:00:00Z
Content: Its not that cut and dry. But generally speaking, yes this makes sense.  There’s always title considerations and nuances, but what you propose here should transfer the ownership from your dad to the trust beneficiaries.

Author: kiheiman
Date: 2025-02-26T05:29:09Z
Content: The mineral rights are leased and I assume that they are producing.  The original lease was from 1981.  The lease was for 3 years unless the wells were producing at the end of three years.

Author: kiheiman
Date: 2025-02-26T05:30:16Z
Content: That seems to be logical.  The Trust Certification makes sense.

Author: kiheiman
Date: 2025-02-26T14:51:05Z
Content: Any recommendations for a NM lawyer that would be reasonable in cost.  It appears that the mineral rights (even though there are producing wells) have little value because 4 acre mineral rights are divided between 250 owners.  My gut feeling right now is to just abandon the situation and do nothing.

Author: James_Garner1
Date: 2025-02-26T14:55:20Z
Content: @Richard_Winbladgives you solid advice. Follow up with a NM attorney on whether the after death filing of the deed is valid before you go further with this issue. It should be a brief consultation on the issue.

Author: fjonesiv
Date: 2025-02-26T15:00:38Z
Content: because 4 acre mineral rights are divided between 250 owners

Author: BlackGold
Date: 2025-02-27T15:06:35Z
Content: I am not an attorney and don’t know a thing about New Mexico, but in Texas almost every title attorney has told me NEVER use a quit claim.  They don’t establish ownership of a property, but dis-ownership.  So you don’t transfer ownership with them.  Basically it is stating, I don’t think I have ownership in this property, but if I do, in the event that I do, I am disclaiming here and now any rights to that ownership.Unfortunately I’ve pretty much seen the FREE 30minute legal consultation go away.  I think because it doesn’t for the most part generate business.  So it just eats up time with no fee.  Maybe in some small town, you find an old time attorney or a new attorney that doesn’t have any business, that will give you a few minutes and give you and idea if it is worth spending more money on.  Otherwise I think you’re looking at $250-$400/hr or more to spend time answering your questions.  Maybe some chance you could go to a free legal clinic at a law school?  Maybe some bar associations might have a free legal clinic.  Not sure you get to spend 2 hours for free at a clinic, but maybe 15-20 minutes with a student lawyer.   I’m thinking you probably need a probate lawyer to transfer title.  Maybe an oil and gas attorney.  You probably need to think about how much revenue is coming in and decide if the juice is worth the squeeze.  If you’re getting $5/month but probate costs you $2500…that sure is a long payback period.  Very possible to let those go and spend the $2500 buying some new producing minerals for a better return?

Author: tim_dowd
Date: 2025-02-27T16:27:23Z
Content: Texas is considered an outlier in the use of quitclaim deeds. There was a case based on a statute that said that a grantee of a quitclaim deed would not be a bona fide purchaser and could  be subject to unrecorded agreements. This is a whack case and whack statute. Texas has now amended the statute that says that after four years, the grantee can be considered a bona fide purchaser.

Author: kiheiman
Date: 2025-02-27T16:47:54Z
Content: IMHO, the mineral rights in New Mexico are not of any value since there are so many owners.  The yearly royalties are miniscule.   My concern is who has legal ownership of the rights. If the rights are in my mother’s trust, then we need to transfer out the rights to someone else so that we can close the trust.  If the rights are not in the trust, then we can close the trust right now.    My father prepared a Quit Claim deed in 2007 for the mineral rights and indicating that the rights should be transferred to his trust.  He died in early 2008.  My mother recorded the deed in Eddy County in late 2008.  A certificate of trust was never recorded, so that in itself could mean that the mineral rights are not in the trust.  I am OK with that.  Worst case, the trust beneficiaries could just ignore the mineral rights and the recorded QCD and close the trust.

Author: kiheiman
Date: 2025-02-27T16:49:56Z
Content: I would be willing to do that if I could find a lawyer that would not charge more than a couple of hours of time.  We know that the current mineral rights have no value, so it would not be logical to spend a lot of money with a lawyer to tell us that the recorded deed is not legal.

Author: kiheiman
Date: 2025-02-27T16:51:58Z
Content: The Quit Claim deeds for the Texas mineral rights were never recorded.  We have the copies.  Since they were never recorded, then it would seem to be fair to assume that the mineral rights are not in the trust.  That means that we do not need to dispose of those mineral rights in order to close the trust.  Same situation for the Oklahoma farm mineral rights.

Author: TennisDaze
Date: 2025-02-27T17:22:07Z
Content: Based on your posts, it appears that your father prepared his own quit claim deed without consulting a New Mexico title attorney.  The QCD was filed by your mother after the grantor’s death, again without consulting a New Mexico attorney.  Adding to this situation, the QCD was to a living trust which may or may not have been properly established in New Mexico. No one can tell you if the QCD is valid without reading the exact wording of the QCD and determining whether or not the QCD complies with the requirements under NM law to transfer title, whether it is effective when filed after death (as there is no NM probate), and also determining the New Mexico status of the trust.  And no lawyer will give you any definitive legal opinion without reading all the documents.  The important lesson here for mineral owners is that is not a good way to handle mineral title.  Saving the up-front legal fees has created more headaches for the heirs who now face higher legal costs to clear it up.

Author: James_Garner1
Date: 2025-02-27T17:51:14Z
Content: Make sure all family members are in agreement on not recording the MD since it has been executed and in your control.

Author: Bob77
Date: 2025-03-02T00:44:29Z
Content: Why in the world would you hire an attorney for a 4/250ths mineral acre interest? It would be fiscally irresponsible to do so unless you just want to prove a point to someone? No reason to spend time nor money on the interest, walk away from it and youll come out ahead.  Hard to do I know, since your parents owned it, but this one of those times where its just not worth it.

Author: James_Garner1
Date: 2025-03-15T23:04:29Z
Content: @Richard_WinbladIn 40+ years I had not seen this issue prior to this post. I just saw it a 2nd time concerning property in CO. I did not review statutes or case law since it did not affect my work. Interesting, but not enough for me to put in the research.

Date: 2025-03-29T23:07:49Z
Content: You say that the yearly royalties are miniscule.  Is it the trust who is receiving the royalties or someone else?

Author: nielloeb
Date: 2025-05-21T15:06:07Z
Content: I know about Earth Point’s “Texas Land Survey - Search By Description.”  But it’s not accurate.  Neither is the TX RRC GIS Viewer measurement tool.

Author: Kitchen
Date: 2025-05-21T15:43:11Z
Content: Historically, Texans have turned to the Texas General Land Office for maps and other tools used to display and organize information about the state’s rich natural resources.Besides historical maps,…

Author: TennisDaze
Date: 2025-05-21T17:49:03Z
Content: RRC and Texas GLO overlay gis viewers are generally accurate as to section locations, but new surveys may show lines somewhat off.  Measurement tools are not designed for exact accuracy.  You can go to GLO Land Grant Database and pull up the scanned records for an abstract which will show original acreage and updates from later patent survey.  Be aware that many sections have multiple abstracts for different parts depending on orignal grantee.  Also, GLO is still working on scanning and so records may not be available.  A lot of well permits are based on ‘called’ acreage from original records, rather than newer resurvey.https://www.glo.texas.gov/archives-heritage/search-our-collections/land-grant-search

rag_documents.title: Tribal Trust land survey
rag_documents.content:
Topic: Tribal Trust land survey

Author: Bobbxys
Date: 2025-04-30T14:14:06Z
Content: I recently inherited mineral rights on 160 acres of tribal trust land. The land is 5 miles West of Minco, OK. Validus Energy offered my aunt and I several hundred thousand for a survey and we signed. We also agreed to a 20% royalty if they drill. I am wondering where exactly we stand as I know almost nothing about mineral rights. Is that a lowball offer for a survey? Is 20% royalty good or bad? It is my understanding that the BIA (Bureau of Indian Affairs) will not accept anything less than 20% royalty on tribal land. They also won’t accept any post production costs or recovery cost clauses in the lease.

Author: Bobbxys
Date: 2025-04-30T18:57:58Z
Content: Thanks a ton for responding! My aunt did not sign an oil lease. (unless she is mistaken, was the $200k a bonus for a drilling lease, possibly?) It was a flat amount for them to survey the land, was my understanding.

Author: TayNeatCPA
Date: 2025-04-30T22:44:04Z
Content: It’s standard practice for the drilling operator to offer a lease bonus to the mineral owners in exchange for the right to extract your minerals. This sounds like what your Aunt received. The 20% royalty is her cut of the oil they extract, if any. They keep the other 80%.

Author: Bobbxys
Date: 2025-04-30T23:00:03Z
Content: Ok, thank you. I am starting to wonder at this point what exactly she signed. I am going to contact her and see if i can get a copy of the agreement.

Author: M_Barnes
Date: 2025-05-01T14:41:53Z
Content: 35-10N-8W- they are probably leasing for a horizontal well or wells.  I moved your post over to the Grady County, OK area as it is more relevant.

Author: Bobbxys
Date: 2025-05-02T21:12:27Z
Content: Thank you! The Mineral Help tab unfortunately is giving me error 404 on every choice in the dropdown box. Not sure what is going on.

Author: M_Barnes
Date: 2025-05-02T23:05:10Z
Content: I tried it and the same thing happened.  I reported it to the administrator.

Author: Bobbxys
Date: 2025-05-09T00:51:46Z
Content: Confirmed with the BIA that this was a mineral lease. $1,250 per acre bonus. 20% royalty. no recovery cost or production cost.

Author: M_Barnes
Date: 2025-05-09T13:14:41Z
Content: Keep that lease copy!  Good to have the correct information.

Author: Bobbxys
Date: 2025-05-20T22:57:03Z
Content: @M_BarnesHello again. I see others talking about leases within units on some other posts, and I was wondering if there was a way to see how much of my 640 unit was already leased, and what sections they might group in a multi-unit. 35 10n 08w grady county

Author: M_Barnes
Date: 2025-05-21T12:56:45Z
Content: Multi unit would probably be with 26 to the north or 2 to the south.
You can checkwww.okcountyrecords.comfor leases in 35.  You might not be able to figure out the net acres as the leases list the gross.  And some companies do not file until the last minute as a strategy.

Author: Bobbxys
Date: 2025-05-21T15:34:44Z
Content: I’m not pulling any mineral leases up for sections 26 or 02. I also noticed my mineral lease isn’t on there, probably because it’s filed and kept through the BIA. It makes me wonder if the neighboring sections are also indian trust land, and not showing up on okcountryrecords for that reason.

Content: We receive royalties on a couple of vertical wells that produce very little and two horizontals that were drilled back in 2018. The horizontals are well into the decline curve. I find it interesting that we have not seen any additional activity in this section while the next section west has at least 10 wells.

Author: M_Barnes
Date: 2025-05-21T12:47:37Z
Content: It could be the geology of the reservoirs, drilling priorities of the operating companies, etc. They have to balance all of their expiration of leases, reservoir pressure on Held By Production (HBP) units, rig availability, frac crews, etc.  Marathon and Gulport had your horizontal wells.  Marathon was just bought by Conoco Phillips, so Conoco may have different priorities.

rag_documents.title: New Wells with existing wells
rag_documents.content:
Topic: New Wells with existing wells

Author: kborak
Date: 2025-05-20T13:44:48Z
Content: We have minerals in an abstract that is currently owned by company A and are older vertical wells that we receive royalties. Company B decides to put in 2 new horizontal wells that will run through the same property but obviously deeper. We haven’t received a lease offer for these. We are listed on the pool P-12 forms. What should we do about this?

Author: TennisDaze
Date: 2025-05-20T14:50:27Z
Content: You need to review your oil and gas lease to see what depths were included and whether there was a release of depths below the existing wells.  Most old leases included all depths.  Some have clause releasing depths below deepest depth drilled or below the producing formation.  Others have no release clause and all depths will be held by the producing wells.

Author: kborak
Date: 2025-05-20T15:06:44Z
Content: Thanks for the clarification. That’s what I thought but wanted to ask to be sure.

Author: kborak
Date: 2025-05-20T15:09:03Z
Content: Another question….since it’s a different operator, would I receive a different DO or would the payments just continue?

Author: Mineral_Owner5
Date: 2025-05-20T15:17:43Z
Content: Be glad that they are at least going to drill two new wells. Good Luck to you Sir!

Author: kborak
Date: 2025-05-20T15:48:30Z
Content: Thank you. I’m definitely glad but just want to make sure I understand everything.

Author: TennisDaze
Date: 2025-05-20T17:01:39Z
Content: You will receive new DO for the new wells.  If the horizontal wells are sharing or allocation wells drilled across your tract or unit and other unrelated tracts, then the DOI will not be the same.

Author: C.RITZ
Date: 2025-05-21T10:08:04Z
Content: That is what I thought and now wait for the mail box money.
